analysis.one_liner: Lets investors shrink capital gains taxes by adjusting the purchase price of long-held assets for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2018 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how capital gains taxes are figured. When someone sells a stock or business asset they have held for more than three years, the bill would raise the taxable purchase price by the amount of inflation since they bought it, shrinking the reported gain and the tax owed. It would apply to individuals, partnerships, S corporations, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and business owners who hold stocks or tangible business property for more than three years would pay less capital gains tax, because inflation would be subtracted from the profit they are taxed on. Because capital gains are realized mostly by higher-income households, the benefit would flow disproportionately to wealthy households. Operators of mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and pass-through businesses would pass the benefit to their shareholders and partners.

how_it_helps.text: For assets held more than three years, the bill increases the taxpayer's 'basis' — the purchase price used to compute taxable gain — by inflation, so gains that merely reflect rising prices are not taxed.

The inflation adjustment applies to individual investors, pass-through businesses such as partnerships and S corporations, and mutual funds and real estate investment trusts, excluding corporations directly.
It applies only to assets acquired after December 31, 2018, and requires written documentation of the original purchase price.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall, since capital gains would be measured after inflation. That cost is spread across all taxpayers through either higher future taxes, more borrowing, or cuts elsewhere, while households whose main asset is a home or a paycheck — which get no similar adjustment — would not share in the benefit.

drawbacks.text: Because capital gains are realized overwhelmingly by higher-income households, the tax cut would concentrate its benefits at the top while shrinking federal revenue that funds other programs.

Indexing only assets held more than three years and requiring written purchase documentation adds complexity, and the bill still lets asset owners escape tax on real economic gains alongside inflation gains.
Indexing basis permanently reduces the price paid for gains relative to wages, which are taxed without any inflation adjustment for bracket value only.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea of not taxing gains that are just inflation has real fairness appeal, but this version's three-year holding requirement means the benefit flows almost entirely to long-term holders of stocks and business real estate — a population that skews wealthy. Because capital gains are mostly realized by high-income households, the cost would land on general revenue that everyone else relies on, while ordinary households' main assets (wages, homes sold within a few years) get little. The anti-abuse rules are a genuine plus, but they don't change the distribution of who gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Devin Nunes introduced the bill on July 19, 2018, with five Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that writes tax legislation.
No further action was taken: no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
It had five cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democratic support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury kept the capital gains revenue the bill would have cut, and long-term asset holders gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; no one else

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat supported it, and no chamber ever voted on it.

industries.industry: Investors in stocks and long-held business assets
industries.note: Wealthy individuals and pass-through business owners holding stocks or business property more than three years would pay less tax on gains. Because capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, the benefit skews to the top.

The bill extends the inflation adjustment through regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, and S corporations, so fund and trust shareholders get the break. Corporate shareholders are excluded.

The government would collect less in capital gains revenue, reducing funds available for other priorities or requiring higher taxes elsewhere. The bill includes an anti-abuse rule allowing the IRS to disallow adjustments arranged principally to inflate the benefit.
